explanations.answer: That God hurry to help him
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. David opens with “Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Hurry, O LORD, to help me!” No warm-up and no long speech. He walks in and says what he needs, twice, and I respect a man who gets to the point.

explanations.answer: That God show him the way to go
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not what David asks for here. His first words are “Make haste, O God, to deliver me!” He wants rescue, and he wants it quick.

That's a real thing to pray, but it isn't how this psalm opens. David's first words are “Make haste, O God, to deliver me!” He's asking for help and rescue right now. The song starts with the emergency.
Yes, friend. David prays, “May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded…” These are people who are after his life, and he asks that they end up ashamed. He brings it to God as a prayer.
The text says it the other way around. David prays, “May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded…” So ashamed is exactly where he asks them to end up. He says it as a prayer to God.

explanations.answer: That they rejoice and be glad in God
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David prays, “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You…” He's just been talking about people who want him gone, and now he turns to the people who want God. His wish for them is joy.

explanations.answer: That they hide until the danger passes
explanations.explanation: Nothing about hiding here, friend. David's wish for everyone who seeks God is, “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You…” He wants them glad, not tucked away. Nobody's ducking under a counter in this verse.

explanations.answer: That they march out and fight beside him
explanations.explanation: No army in this verse. David says, “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You…” His wish for them is gladness in God. The only thing marching in this song is the praise.
That's it. David says to God, “You are my help and my deliverer…” He calls himself poor and needy, and then he says who his help is. He doesn't point to himself.
The psalm doesn't say that, friend. David says, “You are my help and my deliverer…” and he's talking to God. His mighty men don't get that title here.
No sword in this verse. David looks up and says to God, “You are my help and my deliverer…” He's calling himself poor and needy, and then he points to the One who helps.
The text says the opposite. David ends with “O LORD, do not delay.” He's asking God to hurry, so there's no take-your-time in there. That's a man who wants help soon.
That's right. David's last words in Psalm 70 are “O LORD, do not delay.” He started the psalm asking God to hurry and he finishes the same way. The prayer is bookended by hurry.
Yes, friend. The writer prays, “In Your justice, rescue and deliver me…” He's leaning on who God is, not on anything about himself. That's a solid place to stand.
He never brings up his résumé. The writer says, “In Your justice, rescue and deliver me…” He's pointing at God's justice, not at his own track record. That's a good way to ask for help.
No family tree in this verse. The writer prays, “In Your justice, rescue and deliver me…” What he's counting on is God's justice. His family's name doesn't come up.
That's the one. He says to God, “…for You are my rock and my fortress.” Both are things you run to when trouble comes. Rock, fortress, refuge: he's piling up places to be safe.

Those sound like they'd fit, but they aren't the words here. The writer says, “…for You are my rock and my fortress.” A rock and a fortress are places you can stay. You hide in them instead of swinging them.

Nice picture, but those aren't the words in this verse. The writer says, “…for You are my rock and my fortress.” He's asking for a place of safety. Lamps are for the dark, and a fortress is for the danger.
Right on, baker. He says, “I have leaned on You since birth…” He's looking back over his whole life and he can't find a time he wasn't leaning on God. That's a long stretch of leaning.
The writer goes way earlier than that. He says, “I have leaned on You since birth…” A wedding would be a late start by comparison. He's counting from day one.
He doesn't mention a crown at all. The writer says, “I have leaned on You since birth…” His leaning on God starts long before any ceremony. It starts at the very beginning.
That's it. He says, “My mouth is filled with Your praise and with Your splendor all day long.” All day long, friend. That's a mouth with a full schedule and no complaints.
That's not what fills his mouth. He says, “My mouth is filled with Your praise and with Your splendor all day long.” It's praise, and it goes all day.
Not laws in this verse. He says, “My mouth is filled with Your praise and with Your splendor all day long.” What fills his mouth is praise, and he says it goes on all day long.
That's what they say. His enemies say, “God has forsaken him…” Notice who is saying it, friend. It's the enemies talking, and the writer is the one praying for God to stay near.
The enemies don't list any charges here. They say, “God has forsaken him…” They're talking about what they think God has done. It's their claim, and the writer answers it with prayer.

explanations.answer: His friends have turned on him
explanations.explanation: Friends aren't mentioned in this verse. The writer's enemies say, “God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him.” That's what comes from the people lying in wait for him.
Yes, friend. His enemies say no one will rescue him, and he turns to God and prays, “Be not far from me, O God.” He answers their talk with a prayer. That's the right place to take it.
The text says he does ask. Right after the enemies' words, he prays, “Be not far from me, O God.” He doesn't argue with them. He talks to God.
Not quite, friend. Going quiet isn't what he says. He says, “But I will always hope and will praise You more and more.” More and more is the opposite of quiet.
That's right. With accusers around, he says, “But I will always hope and will praise You more and more.” He isn't waiting it out in silence. His praise is turning up, not down.

explanations.answer: He can't know their full measure
explanations.explanation: That's the one. He says he'll declare God's righteousness and salvation all day long, “…though I cannot know their full measure.” It's like trying to find the bottom of a bottomless cookie jar. You keep reaching in, and you never hit the end.

explanations.answer: He has only seen them once
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say that. He says he'll declare them all day long, “…though I cannot know their full measure.” Nothing in the verse says he has seen them only once.

explanations.answer: He has forgotten most of them
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say he forgot. He says he'll declare God's righteousness and salvation all day long, “…though I cannot know their full measure.” It's too much to take in, not too little to remember.
It's the other way around. He says, “I will come in the strength of the Lord GOD…” He's not walking in on his own power. He's bringing God's.
Right, baker. He says, “I will come in the strength of the Lord GOD…” So the strength is God's, not his own. Strong words from a man who earlier prayed about his strength failing.

explanations.answer: Until he tells the next generation of God's power
explanations.explanation: You got it. He prays, “…do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation…” Even old and gray, he has a job left to do. He wants to pass it on.

explanations.answer: Until every one of his enemies is gone
explanations.explanation: That's not what he sets as the finish line. He prays, “…do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation…” What he wants is to tell the next generation. His enemies don't come into it.

explanations.answer: Until he gets to see his home once more
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say anything about home. He prays, “…do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation…” His eyes are on the ones coming after him.

Yes, friend. After talking about the great things God has done, he asks, “Who, O God, is like You?” (Psalm 71:19) I think that's the sound of a man amazed. He's not asking because he's stuck for an answer. He's lifting his eyes to who God is.
That's not his question here. Looking at the great things God has done, he asks, “Who, O God, is like You?” I bet his heart is full of wonder in this verse.

explanations.answer: How long will this go on
explanations.explanation: Not in this verse. After saying God has done great things, he asks, “Who, O God, is like You?” He's looking at who God is.
That's the word. He says, “…You will revive me once again.” He's been honest about the troubles, and he still says it. That's a hope with some weight on it.
Not that one, friend. He says, “…You will revive me once again.” The word is revive, not test. He says it right after naming his many troubles and misfortunes.
He says the opposite. He says, “…You will revive me once again.” The man who prayed not to be forsaken is saying God will revive him.
That's right. He says, “You will increase my honor and comfort me once again.” After the troubles, he's looking ahead to honor and comfort. That's a good thing to hold on to.
The text says he does say it. He says, “You will increase my honor and comfort me once again.” That's his hope after all those troubles.
Right on, baker. He says, “So I will praise You with the harp for Your faithfulness, O my God…” He brings the harp and the lyre, and he brings the reason too. It's God's faithfulness.
The harp isn't for a harvest here. He says, “So I will praise You with the harp for Your faithfulness, O my God…” What he's praising God for is His faithfulness.
No money talk in this verse. He says, “So I will praise You with the harp for Your faithfulness, O my God…” The song is about God's faithfulness, not what's in anyone's pockets.

That's the one. He says, “When I sing praise to You my lips will shout for joy, along with my soul, which You have redeemed.” His lips and his soul are shouting together. The whole man is in the song.
No choir in this verse. He says his lips will shout for joy, “…along with my soul, which You have redeemed.” The one who joins in is his own soul.
He doesn't bring in a crowd here. He says his lips will shout for joy, “…along with my soul, which You have redeemed.” It's his soul that joins in, and it's a joyful one.
